evidence: Cic. Att. 2.2.1: cūrā, amābō tē, Cicerōnem nostrum
Quint. 10.1.93: satura quidem tōta nostra est
terms.comment: Agrees with the thing owned. “Ours” is the same word as a predicate: tōta nostra est. Of family and friends it is affectionate, “our dear …”: Cicerōnem nostrum, our boy. Left out where the owner is plain: dēsīderātōque acquiēscimus lectō, we rest in the bed we longed for (our bed).

phrases.english: Do look after our boy Cicero, please.

phrases.latin: ō quid solūtīs est beātius cūrīs, cum mēns onus repōnit, ac peregrīnō labōre fessī vēnimus larem ad nostrum, dēsīderātōque acquiēscimus lectō?
phrases.english: Oh, what is more blessed than cares set free, when the mind lays down its load, and tired from labour abroad we come to our own hearth and rest in the bed we longed for?
Satire, at least, is wholly ours.

phrases.latin: quid vōs hīc? inquam, num fēriae sēmentīvae ōtiōsōs hūc addūxērunt, ut patrēs et avōs solēbant nostrōs?
phrases.english: What are you all doing here? I said. Has the sowing holiday brought you here at leisure, as it used to bring our fathers and grandfathers?

phrases.latin: Pater noster, quī es in caelīs, sānctificētur nōmen tuum.
phrases.english: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-catullus, loci-cicero-epistulae, loci-quintilianus, loci-varro, loci-vulgata), checked against the editions named there.
